results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The stated finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space and convex set.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set is strictly separated from that set by a nonzero linear functional.

[F2] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean coordinates identify linear functionals with vectors and give the usual unit sphere.

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum.

[F5] [[lem-finite-dimensional-unit-spheres-are-sequentially-compact]]: unit spheres in finite-dimensional normed spaces are sequentially compact without a choice principle.

[F6] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]: rational coordinates are dense in real coordinates.

[F7] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]] supplies the positive real sequence $\epsilon_m=1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(m))$, $m\in\mathbb N$, decreasing to zero with the canonical-natural field convention.



1.1 Fix affine coordinates $H\cong\mathbb R^k$. Closure preserves convexity without choosing approximating sequences: for $x,y\in K$ and any $\epsilon>0$, choose two points of $C$ within $\epsilon$ of them; their convex combination approximates $(1-t)x+ty$ within $\epsilon$, so this point lies in $K$. Enumerate rational $k$-tuples canonically by increasing sums of absolute numerators and positive denominators, breaking the finite ties lexicographically. Density [F6] and the open complement of $K$ show that for each $m\in\mathbb N$ at least one enumerated point lies in $B(z,\epsilon_m)\setminus K$. Let $z_m$ be the first such point. This is a uniquely specified sequence with $z_m\to z$, not a countable selection of arbitrary witnesses. [given, F3, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 The nonempty compact set $K\cap\overline B(z_m,\|z_m-z\|+1)$ contains $z$. By [F2] and [F4], squared distance to $z_m$ attains a minimum there, and every point outside that ball is farther than the candidate $z$. Thus a nearest point $q_m\in K$ exists. It is unique: if two distinct minimizers had squared distance $d_m^2$, their midpoint would have squared distance $d_m^2-\|q_m-q'_m\|^2/4$, contradicting minimality and convexity. Consequently $(q_m)$ is also canonically determined. Since $z_m\notin K$, put $u_m=(z_m-q_m)/\|z_m-q_m\|$. Expanding the distance at $q_m+t(q-q_m)$ and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $u_m\cdot(q-q_m)\le0$ for every $q\in K$. Also $\|q_m-z\|\le2\|z_m-z\|\to0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every $u_m$ has norm one. The exact choice-free sequential-compactness supplier [F5] gives a subsequence converging to a unit vector $u$. This introduces no additional choice hypothesis. [F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For every $q\in K$, pass to the limit in $u_m\cdot(q-q_m)\le0$ along that subsequence. Continuity of the Euclidean pairing and $q_m\to z$ give $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The unit vector $u$ defines a nonzero supporting functional for $K$, hence for $C$, at $z$. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The nonempty compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, continuous entropy map $s$, prescribed $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, coordinatewise integral convention, and feasibility of every Borel probability mixture with that barycenter. The normalization is per mole and no system-size limit is taken.

[A1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: A generator point is a model-specified state label; the theorem's mixture feasibility is an additional model assumption and does not assert that every phase collection is physically available.

[A2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: Entropy is a finite state function on the declared physical states. Continuity of $s$ on this compact $K$ is the explicit regularity hypothesis here.

[F1] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and [[def-probability-measure]]: The Borel sigma algebra is generated by the relatively open subsets of $K$, and each probability measure has total mass one.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] and [[lem-tdmath-measure-integral-agrees-with-root-lebesgue-integral]]: The local nonnegative integral is the supremum of simple-function integrals and agrees with the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral. Since both signed-integral conventions use the difference of the positive and negative part integrals, they agree on bounded real functions as well.

[F3] [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], and [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]: Bounded Borel real functions are integrable under a finite probability measure; their integrals are linear, order-preserving, and satisfy $|\int f\,dP|\le\int|f|\,dP$.

[L1] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded and attains its minimum and maximum.

[L2] [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]], and [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: Continuous images of compact metric spaces are compact; compact Euclidean subsets are closed and bounded; closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces are compact.

[L3] [[thm-rank-nullity]]: For a linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces, domain dimension equals kernel dimension plus image dimension.



**Given:** The data in [A1]–[A2] and [F1]–[F3]. Write $h:K\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ for the continuous map $h(x)=(x,s(x))$, and let $H:=h[K]$ and $C:=\operatorname{conv}H$, where convex hull means finite convex combinations.

1.1 The map $h$ is continuous, so [L2] makes $H$ compact. For every Borel probability $P$ on $K$, each coordinate of $h$ is bounded and Borel. Compactness and [L1] give boundedness. If $|f|\le M$ for one such coordinate, [F3] gives $\int_K|f|\,dP\le M P(K)=M$, so $f$ is integrable. [given, F1, F3, L1, L2, construct]

2.1 Every point of $C$ is a finite convex combination of points $h(x_i)$. If such a representation has $N>d+2$, the linear map $T:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+2}$ defined by $T(c)=(\sum_i c_i h(x_i),\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector $c$ by [L3], because the coordinate bases give domain dimension $N$ and codomain dimension $d+2$. Thus $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i h(x_i)=0$, so $c$ has both positive and negative coordinates. After dropping zero weights from the representation, set $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace each weight $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. The new weights remain nonnegative, still sum to one, represent the same point, and at least one is zero. Repeating reduces every combination to at most $d+2$ terms. Hence $C$ is the image of $K^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$ under $\Theta((x_i),(\theta_i))=\sum_{i=1}^{d+2}\theta_i h(x_i)$, where $\Delta_{d+2}:=\{(\theta_i):\theta_i\ge0,\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; shorter combinations are padded with zero weights and any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Each factor $K$ is closed and bounded by [L2], and $\Delta_{d+2}$ is closed by continuity of the finite coordinate sum and its coordinate inequalities; it is bounded since $0\le\theta_i\le1$. Their product is therefore closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{(d+1)(d+2)}$, so compact by [L2]. To check $\Theta$ is continuous on this compact parameter set, fix a parameter $((x_i),(\theta_i))$. Each coordinate $h_j$ is bounded by some $M$ on $K$ and is continuous at each of the finitely many $x_i$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose neighborhoods of the $x_i$ making $|h_j(x_i')-h_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/(2N)$ for every output coordinate $j$, and require $|\theta_i'-\theta_i|<\epsilon/(2N(M+1))$. Since $0\le\theta_i'\le1$ and $|h_j(x_i)|\le M$, each product difference $|\theta_i'h_j(x_i')-\theta_ih_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/N$; summing over $i$ makes each output-coordinate difference smaller than $\epsilon$. Thus $\Theta$ is continuous. The continuous-image clause of [L2] makes its image $C$ compact, and [L2] also makes $C$ closed. [given, L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Fix any Borel probability $P$ on $K$ and let $y(P):=(\int_K x\,dP,\int_Ks\,dP)=\int_Kh\,dP$, with coordinatewise integration. For $\epsilon>0$, compactness of $H$ gives a finite cover of $H$ by open Euclidean balls of radius $\epsilon$. Their preimages under $h$ are Borel; disjointifying them in a fixed finite order gives a finite Borel partition $(A_i)$ of $K$. For every nonempty part choose $z_i\in A_i$ and put $\theta_i=P(A_i)$. Then $y_\epsilon:=\sum_i\theta_i h(z_i)$ belongs to $C$. For $x\in A_i$, both $h(x)$ and $h(z_i)$ lie in the same radius-$\epsilon$ ball, so each coordinate difference is at most $2\epsilon$. The simple map equal to $h(z_i)$ on $A_i$ has integral $y_\epsilon$ by the simple-integral definition. By linearity and the integral triangle inequality in [F3], each coordinate of $y(P)-y_\epsilon$ has absolute value at most $2\epsilon\sum_iP(A_i)=2\epsilon$. Consequently $\|y(P)-y_\epsilon\|_2\le2\epsilon\sqrt{d+1}$, so the sequence obtained with $\epsilon=1/n$ converges to $y(P)$. Since $C$ is closed by step 2.1, $y(P)\in C$. [given, F1, F2, F3, L2, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 Because $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, a finite convex combination of generators has barycenter $\bar x$; its corresponding combination of points $h(x)$ shows that $E_{\bar x}:=\{r\in\mathbb R:(\bar x,r)\in C\}$ is nonempty. The set $E_{\bar x}$ is bounded because $C$ is bounded, and it is closed because $C$ is closed and $r\mapsto(\bar x,r)$ is continuous. By [L2] it is compact in $\mathbb R$, so [L1] applied to the identity function yields a maximum $r_*\in E_{\bar x}$. [given, L1, L2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Represent $(\bar x,r_*)\in C$ by a finite convex combination $\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i(x_i,s(x_i))$, dropping zero weights. If $N>d+1$, the linear map $R:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ given by $R(c)=(\sum_i c_ix_i,\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector by [L3], since its domain dimension is $N$ and its codomain dimension is $d+1$. Hence $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_ix_i=0$, with both signs among the $c_i$. If $\sum_i c_is(x_i)\ne0$, choose the sign of $c$ so that this sum is positive. For sufficiently small $t>0$, the weights $\theta_i+tc_i$ are nonnegative, preserve total mass and barycenter, and increase the last coordinate above $r_*$, contradicting maximality in step 3.2. Thus $\sum_i c_is(x_i)=0$. Now take $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. This removes at least one positive weight while preserving total mass, barycenter, and entropy value $r_*$. Repeating finitely many times leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights. [given, L3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 Let $P_*:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ be the probability measure from step 4.1. Each $\delta_{x_i}$ is countably additive because among disjoint Borel sets at most one contains $x_i$, and $\delta_{x_i}(K)=1$; hence $P_*$ is a Borel probability measure. It has barycenter $\bar x$ and entropy $r_*$, so it is feasible by the model assumption. For any other feasible Borel probability $P$, step 3.1 gives $(\bar x,\int s\,dP)\in C$, so $\int s\,dP\le r_*$. Thus $P_*$ attains the entropy maximum among all Borel mixtures and has at most $d+1$ atoms. No finite generator menu was assumed. [given, A1, F1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎



The proof treats every feasible Borel probability mixture, not just finite mixtures. It proves that the vector of integrated generator coordinates and entropy lies in a compact finite-dimensional convex hull, then uses maximality at the prescribed barycenter to reduce the support to $d+1$. It does not establish that a physical system has a compact generator domain or that every mathematical mixture is physically feasible; those remain explicit model hypotheses.

**Given:** The equilibrium-coordinate convention of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], the contact restrictions of [[def-td-thermal-contact-constraints]], the feasible-set definition [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]], and the entropy and equilibrium-maximum postulates.

[F1] Each adopted entropy is a finite scalar measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

[F2] On every specified convex region the entropy is continuous and satisfies the stated Jensen concavity inequality ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

[F3] The admitted separated pairs form a designated subset $\mathcal C_{AB}\subseteq D_A\times D_B$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]]).

[F4] Under the composition map, the dimensioned total energy of an admitted pair is $U_{A\sqcup B}=U_A+U_B$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]]).

[F5] For admitted independent separated macroscopic systems, entropy is additive under the composition map ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

[F6] The tagged bulk family scales its extensive coordinates by $\lambda>0$, and the entropy postulate assumes $S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]], [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

[F7] An equilibrium feasible set may be noncompact and need not contain an entropy maximizer ([[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]).

[F8] Stable equilibrium in this route requires an attained global maximum on the exact feasible set ([[post-td-entropy-maximum]]).

[L1] For every real $t$ there is a natural number $n\ge1$ with $t<n$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[L2] The range of every nonempty finite list of real numbers has a greatest member ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]).

[L3] On $\mathbb R^6$, the Euclidean norm is defined by the sum of coordinate squares and induces the usual Euclidean metric ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[L4] A real number $u$ is the supremum of a set $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ exactly when it is an upper bound of $E$ and $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$ of $E$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

[A1] $D_A=D_B=(0,\infty)^3$ in dimensionless $(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)$ coordinates, with each full domain designated as an open single-phase chart; $\hat V_A,\hat V_B,\hat n_A,\hat n_B>0$ are fixed; total energy is $1\,\mathrm J$; every pair $\phi(x)$ in $\mathcal F=\{\phi(x):0<x<1\}$ is admitted in $\mathcal C_{AB}$; $s_*=1\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; and $S_A=2s_*\hat U_A$, $S_B=s_*\hat U_B$, with the same formulas on each tagged scaled copy.

[A2] Compactness uses the inherited Euclidean topology: every cover of $\mathcal F$ by relatively open subsets must have a finite subcover.



**Given:** The model [A1], the compactness convention [A2], facts [F1]–[F8], and [L1]–[L4].

1.1 Each entropy in [A1] is finite, affine and continuous on the convex domain $(0,\infty)^3$, hence concave; it is $C^2$ with $S_{A,U}=2\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$ and $S_{B,U}=1\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. Scaling every extensive coordinate by $\lambda$ scales each entropy by $\lambda$, and the admitted separated-system total is their sum. The pairs in [A1] are admitted by [F3], their fixed total energy uses the composition rule [F4], the separated entropy is the sum by [F5], and the tagged scaling is homogeneous by [F6]. Thus the model satisfies [F1]–[F6]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 For each integer $n\ge2$, put $\mathcal U_n=\{\phi(x)\in\mathcal F:x<1-1/n\}$. It is relatively open: if $\phi(x)\in\mathcal U_n$, then $\epsilon=1-1/n-x>0$, and any $\phi(y)\in\mathcal F$ with $\|\phi(y)-\phi(x)\|_2<\epsilon$ has coordinate difference $\phi(y)-\phi(x)=(y-x,0,0,-(y-x),0,0)$. By [L3], $\|\phi(y)-\phi(x)\|_2=\sqrt2|y-x|$, so $|y-x|<\epsilon$ and $y<1-1/n$. Given any $x\in(0,1)$, [L1] applied to $1/(1-x)>1$ gives an integer $n>1/(1-x)$; then $n\ge2$ and $x<1-1/n$, so the $\mathcal U_n$ cover $\mathcal F$. For any nonempty finite subfamily with indices $n_1,\ldots,n_k$, [L2] gives a greatest index $N$, and its union is $\mathcal U_N$. The feasible state $\phi(1-1/(2N))$ belongs to $\mathcal F$ but not $\mathcal U_N$, so this cover has no finite subcover. By [A2] and [F7], $\mathcal F$ is noncompact and has no assumed attainment guarantee. [given, A1, A2, F7, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

2.1 For every $x\in(0,1)$, the entropy value is $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=s_*(1+x)<2s_*$ because $s_*>0$. Thus $2s_*$ is an upper bound of the feasible entropy values. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Given any $\varepsilon>0$, apply [L1] to $2+s_*/\varepsilon$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/\varepsilon$. Then $x_n:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $$0<2s_*-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x_n))=s_*/n<\varepsilon.$$ Hence feasible entropy values lie arbitrarily close to $2s_*$ from below. [given, A1, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Let $u$ be any upper bound of the feasible entropy values. If $u<2s_*$, set $d:=2s_*-u>0$ and apply [L1] to $2+s_*/d$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/d$. Then $x:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=2s_*-s_*/n>2s_*-d=u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound. Therefore $2s_*\le u$ for every upper bound $u$. By [L4], $\sup\{S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x)):0<x<1\}=2s_*$. [given, A1, L1, L4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.4 For every $x\in(0,1)$, $y=(x+1)/2$ also lies in $(0,1)$ and satisfies $y>x$. Hence $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(y))=s_*(1+y)>s_*(1+x)=S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))$ because $s_*>0$. No feasible state maximizes entropy; the supremum $2s_*$ is not attained because $x=1$ is excluded. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F8] stable equilibrium in this route requires an attained global maximum on the exact feasible set. Since no maximum is attained, this model has no stable equilibrium under that criterion. [F8, step 2.4] ∎

**Given:** AC, dimension $d\geq1$, $\lambda>0$, the cell-product law $Q_\lambda$, and pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_j$.

[A1] AC is part of the Poisson reference construction and of its countable product existence ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F1] On each unit cell, the count has law $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ and, conditional on $n$, the points are independent uniform points subsequently sorted. Finite cell families are independent ([[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F2] The number of length-$n$ label sequences with category counts $(n_0,\ldots,n_s)$ is the multinomial coefficient, and its finite expansion is the multinomial theorem ([[def-multinomial-coefficient]], [[thm-multinomial-theorem]]).

[F3] Exponentials turn sums into products ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]).

[F4] The configuration sigma-algebra is generated by bounded-Borel count maps, finite count cylinders form a generating pi-system, and agreement there determines probability laws ([[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

[F5] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: the real exponential is its everywhere convergent factorial power series. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] permits expectations of increasing nonnegative partial sums and countable sums.



**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables. [A1, step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent. [A1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Put $\theta=\lambda|A|$. The count mass in step 3.1 gives, by nonnegative partial sums and [F5], $$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{an}e^{-\theta}\frac{\theta^n}{n!}=e^{-\theta}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta e^a)^n}{n!}=\exp\!\left(\theta(e^a-1)\right).$$ For $\theta=0$, the count is zero almost surely and both sides are one, so no ambiguous zero power is needed. This establishes the exponential-moment interface before entropy estimates use it. [A1, F3, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves. [A1, step 3.1, F4]

5.1 For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. Thus the laws agree on every finite count cylinder. These cylinders generate the configuration sigma-algebra by [F4], and pi-lambda uniqueness identifies the laws. The one-set count law gives $E_{Q_\lambda}N_A=\lambda|A|$ for bounded $A$. For arbitrary Borel $A$, increase bounded cubes to all space and apply [F5] to the counting measures and Lebesgue measure to obtain the same extended identity. For disjoint Borel $A_n$, the pointwise counting identity $N_{\cup_n A_n}=\sum_nN_{A_n}$ and [F5] show countable additivity of $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}$, while the empty set has expectation zero. Thus the defined intensity functional is a measure and equals $\lambda$ times Lebesgue measure. [A1, step 3.1, F4, F5] ∎

**Given:** The reduced model and domain in the Example, with $P_c,V_c,T_c>0$.

[A1] The isothermal local mechanical-stability criterion for this model is not needed for the calculation below. The claimed result is only the sign of the model derivative.

[F1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: A phase branch and its chart are model-specified; a branch equation is not asserted to be universal.



1.1 At fixed $t$, differentiating the rational equation gives $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial v}=-\frac{24t}{(3v-1)^2}+\frac{6}{v^3}. $$ At $t=0.9$ and $v=1$, this derivative is $-24(0.9)/4+6=0.6>0$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The second derivative is $\partial_v^2p=144t/(3v-1)^3-18/v^4$. At a simultaneous zero, the first derivative gives $t=(3v-1)^2/(4v^3)$ and the second gives $t=(3v-1)^3/(8v^4)$. Equality and $v>1/3$ imply $2v=3v-1$, hence $v=1$, $t=1$, and $p=1$. Conversely these values make both derivatives zero. Thus $T_c$ is the model critical temperature in this stated sense, and $t=0.9<1$ is below it. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The derivative is continuous near $(t,v)=(0.9,1)$ because $3v-1\ne0$ there. Hence it remains positive on some open neighborhood within $v>1/3$. Since $P=P_cp$ and $V=V_cv$ with positive scales, $(\partial P/\partial V)_T=(P_c/V_c)(\partial p/\partial v)_t>0$ there as well. This verifies a positive-slope branch of this phenomenological model only. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The positive divergent core, regular far tail, fixed $z,\beta>0$, and a fixed finite tempering constant $t$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: stability gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$ for every nonzero separation, and the far pair interaction is bounded in absolute value by a decreasing integrable envelope $\psi$ outside some radius $R_0$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: the cell envelope is summable, and the diagonal tail choice has $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and $(\ell/g(\ell))^d\eta(g(\ell))\to0$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for the genuine core there is an increasing finite-valued $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,\infty)$ with $h(0)=0$, $h(m)/m^2\to\infty$, and $H\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$ on unit cells. Translation invariance gives the same inequality for the centered cells $C_i$ used here.

[A2] Boundary-inclusive physical model: for the boundary route only, the model declares a state domain containing the zero-amount state at $\xi_*$ and finite C1 maps $\bar U_c,\bar V_c,\bar S_c:U\to\mathbb R$ with units J, $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and $\Phi=\bar U_c+p_0\bar V_c-T_0\bar S_c$. Its isolated compound has an exact feasible set of tuples $(\xi,y_R,y_B)$ whose projection onto extents is $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$, fixed total energy $\bar U_c(\xi)+E_R(y_R)+E_B(y_B)$, ideal-reservoir entropy $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$, constant store entropy, and pressure-store relation $E_B(y_B)-p_0\bar V_c(\xi)=C_B$ throughout that feasible set. The endpoint corresponding to $\xi_*$ is an attained global maximum of the sum of system, reservoir, and store entropies on this exact set. These are explicit additional model premises, not consequences of the positive-mole state domain.

[F1] [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]]: For an admitted closed process record with the specified ideal reservoir and pressure store, its system potential decreases on every record; an attained global entropy maximum on that exact isolated-compound feasible set gives a global minimum on the projected system state set. For this interior application, that projection contains the system states corresponding to every extent in $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. The supplier does not cover zero amounts outside $D_c$.

[F2] [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]: On a valid single-phase energy-representation and Gibbs natural-variable chart, $dG=-S\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$. The identity is used only at positive amounts; at the boundary, [A1] is the separate derivative premise.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-stoichiometric-tangent-cone]]: For the nonnegative stoichiometric feasible polyhedron, the tangent cone consists exactly of $h$ with $(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for every active species. At a differentiable local minimum, the directional derivative is nonnegative on that cone; for a differentiable convex objective on a convex domain, this condition is sufficient for a global minimum.



1.1 In the positive-amount case, [F1] gives a local minimum of $\Phi$ relative to the exact reaction-feasible states near $\xi_*$. [given, F1]

1.2 In the boundary case, fixed total energy and $E_B-p_0\bar V_c=C_B$ in [A2] give $E_R=C_1-\bar U_c(\xi)-p_0\bar V_c(\xi)$ for a constant $C_1$. Therefore the sum of system and reservoir entropies, plus the constant store entropy, is $S_{\rm tot}=C_0+\bar S_c(\xi)-(\bar U_c(\xi)+p_0\bar V_c(\xi))/T_0=C_0-\Phi(\xi)/T_0$ on the exact boundary-inclusive feasible set. Since $T_0>0$, an attained global entropy maximum at $\xi_*$ is a global, hence local, minimum of $\Phi$ there. [given, A2, algebra]

2.1 Thus in either case $\xi_*$ is a local minimum relative to $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Apply [F3] at $\xi_*$. It identifies the feasible tangent directions as exactly those $h$ satisfying $(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for all $j\in J_*$. The differentiable local-minimum inequality gives $D\Phi(\xi_*)[h]\ge0$ on this cone; substituting [A1]'s gradient identity gives $(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*))\cdot h\ge0$. [given, A1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 If $J_*=\varnothing$, every sufficiently small direction of either sign is feasible, so the tangent cone is $\mathbb R^R$. Put $a:=\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*)$. The inequality in step 3.1 applies to $h=-a$, giving $-|a|^2\ge0$ and therefore $a=0$. [given, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\Phi$ is convex and differentiable on a convex neighborhood containing the relevant feasible set, the sufficiency clause of [F3] makes the tangent inequality sufficient for global minimization there. Without convexity this sufficiency conclusion is not asserted. [given, F3, step 3.1] ∎



For the interior route, the potential minimum follows from the admitted process record and its reservoir/store model. A boundary point with a zero species amount is not in the positive-mole chart. The boundary route therefore needs the explicitly extended entropy and endpoint model in [A2]; a finite C1 extension of $\Phi$ alone would not establish physical stable equilibrium.
